title: Sort-time electrothermal annealing heals leakage-tail cells individually
idea: TRIZ #10 Preliminary action: fix the defect before the part ships. At wafer sort, cells flagged as retention-tail are driven with short high-current pulses through their own and neighbouring access transistors to self-heat the junction region to several hundred C for microseconds, annealing the specific trap responsible, then retested; cells that still fail fall back to row repair.
why: Turns tail cells into normal cells (Fact 3), shrinking repair overhead and permitting longer refresh, while recovering yield, a direct capacity lever.

title: Ecological niche partitioning: retention-binned memory SKUs for matching workloads
idea: Species partition niches instead of competing for one; test-sort dies by measured retention tail into 'arctic' (certified 256 ms tREFI, premium for inference/HBM), standard, and 'ephemeral' (short retention, cheap, sold for TTL activation buffers), with the certified tREFI exposed in a JEDEC mode register.
why: Monetizes the retention distribution instead of designing to the worst tail, and turns dies now downgraded into sellable ephemeral bits (+3-8% yield-equivalent supply).

title: Fractional-reserve banking: row-parity reserve absorbs fluorine-free process's wider tail
idea: Banks keep only a fraction of deposits on hand because withdrawals rarely coincide. Accept the wider retention tail of a hydrogen-passivated, fluorine-free process by adding one XOR parity row per 32-row group inside each subarray; refresh at an interval where at most one row per group is likely to hold a decayed cell, and rebuild that row from parity when ECC flags it.
why: Sets refresh near the 99.99th-percentile cell instead of the 6-sigma tail: 2-4x fewer refreshes (fact 3) for ~3% area, turning the constraint's yield penalty into design margin.

title: Self-healing traps: on-die microheaters anneal leakage defects in the field
idea: Inverts 'aging only makes leakage worse': embed a deuterium-loaded SiN reservoir and a TiN microheater per mat; in scheduled idle windows (data migrated to a spare mat) heat the mat for milliseconds so deuterium diffuses to and passivates the dangling-bond traps that cause trap-assisted junction leakage, resetting the retention tail.
why: Keeps the leakage tail near fresh-wafer levels for life (fact 3), allowing a permanently ~4x longer refresh interval, and partially heals hammer-induced trap generation (fact 9).

title: Post-package repair as a scalpel for the retention tail
idea: DDR4 and DDR5 already expose soft and hard post-package repair for hard faults. Repurpose it: profile in the field, remap the few rows per bank whose retention is below 256 ms onto spare rows, and run the module at 2-4x tREFI with ECC and patrol scrub as a safety net. Needs BIOS/BMC firmware and a validation lab, ~$400k over 18 months.
why: The refresh interval is dictated by a ~1e-6 fraction of cells. Removing that fraction moves the interval toward median retention (seconds) on existing parts (fact 3); the spare-row count caps how far this goes.

title: High-pressure deuterium anneal of purchased finished DRAM wafers
idea: Interface and dangling-bond traps near storage junctions drive SRH tail leakage, and Si-D bonds resist depassivation better than Si-H. Buy finished DRAM wafers or known-good-die lots, run 20 atm D2 anneals at 350-400 C in a rented high-pressure furnace, and measure the retention-tail shift against control wafers. ~$300-500k including test, 15 months.
why: If the tail compresses even 2x, vendors can adopt a single back-end anneal step for 2x longer refresh (fact 3).

title: Toaster-pulse anneals heal retention-tail traps in the field
idea: Random stimulus 'toaster': short hot bursts restore crispness. Embed resistive heater lines in each mat under a deuterium-loaded nitride cap; during maintenance windows a microsecond-scale pulse heats the array locally to ~350 C, releasing deuterium that re-passivates the interface traps behind variable-retention-time cells and aged GIDL tails.
why: Turns the retention tail from a fixed guardband into something repairable; healing aged traps could hold refresh at fresh-die rates and reclaim 2-4x retention margin over life (fact 3).

title: Junkyard-magnet gettering band under every array mat
idea: Random stimulus 'junkyard crane magnet': pull the scrap out before it does damage. Form a carbon-implanted, oxygen-precipitate gettering band 1-2 um below each mat that captures Fe, Cu and Ni atoms which would otherwise sit in junctions as single deep-level traps, the usual root of fA-scale retention-tail outliers.
why: Rare tail cells are often single-defect SRH sites; proximity gettering shrinks the tail population ~10x (fact 3) so refresh can slow for every cell.

title: Wordline Joule self-annealing heals the retention tail yearly
idea: Time shift from a one-time fab anneal to in-field anneals every year, and scale shift to a single row: in maintenance windows the controller drives DC current along selected buried wordlines (small potential difference between both ends) to heat the access region locally to ~250-300 C for milliseconds, annealing the metastable defects behind VRT cells found by retention profiling.
why: Leakage tail/refresh (fact 3) and lifetime drift: removing the worst ~0.01% of cells lets the refresh-bin floor rise ~2x and reverses aging-induced tail growth.

title: Tail rows exiled to an on-die SRAM jail
idea: Scale shift: the ppm-scale retention tail is served by a tiny memory with a different timescale; rows or 64 B segments failing a 1 s retention test at sort or in the field are remapped through a CAM into a few hundred KB of on-die SRAM or fast-refresh eDRAM, letting the rest of the array run at 1 s refresh.
why: Refresh (fact 3): ~16x fewer refresh ops for <0.5% die area, because the long tail sits in ~1e-5 of rows.

title: HMC logic die justified by per-subarray negative-wordline tuning
idea: Micron's Hybrid Memory Cube died because bandwidth alone did not pay back the cost of its logic base die. Make the logic die earn its keep through leakage control. It holds per-subarray DACs and canary cells, measures the retention tail continuously, and sets each subarray's negative wordline voltage and refresh rate through hybrid-bond vias.
why: Leakage tails are local, so per-subarray NWL and refresh tuning is claimed to cut refresh energy and GIDL 2-4x versus one chip-wide setting. It also moves control logic off the DRAM die, where periphery takes 49% of the area.

title: Retired hyperscale DIMMs re-certified with a per-module retention passport
idea: Second-hand DRAM has not won trust because buyers cannot see a module's wear or retention. A test cell measures each retired DIMM's retention tail at temperature and writes a module-specific refresh multiplier and a weak-row list into its SPD. Modules with leakier access transistors then run at 2x refresh instead of being scrapped.
why: Raises usable memory supply through recycling during a ~4x price spike, handling the leakage tail with per-module refresh instead of discard.

title: Certify, don't fabricate: an R4 retention-grade standard and test lab
idea: 10-person constraint: create a market signal instead of a device. Define an open 'R4' grade (passes 256 ms at 85 C with ECC, VRT-screened over 3 thermal cycles) and run a small certification lab with FPGA testers. Hyperscalers and BIOS vendors auto-enable 4x tREFI for R4-labelled modules, so suppliers compete on their retention tail.
why: Fact 3: creates commercial pull for tail reduction and unlocks ~75% refresh savings fleet-wide through policy and a 10-person lab.

title: Spacecraft residue-number codes for error-tolerant numeric storage
idea: Fault-tolerant spacecraft arithmetic used redundant residue number systems. Store integers and quantized weights as residues modulo small coprimes plus two redundant moduli in rows running at 1% BER; a corrupted residue is located and corrected via the Chinese Remainder Theorem, and add/multiply run on residues without decoding.
why: Facts 3 and 5: refresh drops to the 1% quantile and the same redundancy protects in-memory arithmetic; ~25-35% overhead, competitive with ECC because compute stays carry-free.

title: NVDIMM-N failure fixed with printed zinc battery self-refresh
idea: NVDIMM-N modules died on the cost of their flash, supercapacitors and backup controller. Laminate a printed zinc-manganese battery film onto the DIMM that keeps the DRAM in self-refresh through a power loss for minutes to an hour, with no copy to flash.
why: Makes DRAM survive outages for pennies per module, so servers can drop a separate persistence tier. Refresh is carried by stored energy instead of a flash backup.

title: Eliminate single-device isolation: stacked series access transistors exploiting stack effect
idea: Replace the single access FET with two series vertical FETs sharing one gate; in the off state the middle node floats up, giving the upper device negative Vgs and reduced Vds (the logic stack effect) and cutting subthreshold leakage ~10x. Vertical stacking keeps the 4F^2 footprint.
why: ~10x lower leakage gives ~10x longer refresh period with known silicon processing (fact 3).

title: Class-D amplifier efficiency for wordline supplies: inductive switched VPP
idea: Adapted from the class-D audio amplifier's switch from linear to switched-mode conversion: replace the on-die Dickson charge pumps that make VPP (~3 V) and the negative wordline voltage with an inductor-based buck-boost converter using package-embedded inductors, at 70-85% efficiency instead of ~25-35%.
why: Every refresh activation draws wordline charge from VPP; generating that charge 2-3x more efficiently cuts refresh and standby power substantially (facts 3, 10) without touching the cell.

title: Low-melt alloy latent-heat pockets in HBM dummy-bump cavities
idea: Effect: latent heat of fusion. Sealed dummy-bump and dummy-TSV cavities are filled with a 60-70 C Bi-In-Sn eutectic that melts during compute bursts, clamping DRAM die temperature below the 85 C refresh-doubling threshold for tens of seconds and refreezing in idle. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Refresh bandwidth (fact 3): keeps refresh at 1x during bursts (+10-20% peak bandwidth) with no power draw.

title: Photocopier-drum physics: optically gated photoconductor access switch
idea: Adapted from xerography, where a photoreceptor holds surface charge for minutes in the dark and discharges only where light hits: the access element is a wide-bandgap photoconductor (e.g., ZnO or a-SiC) switched by light pulses from an on-chip silicon-nitride waveguide 'wordline'. With no gate electrode there is no gate-induced drain leakage and no wordline CV^2.
why: Wide-bandgap photoconductor dark resistivity can exceed 1e14 ohm-cm, giving sub-aA hold leakage (fact 3) and removing the 3 V wordline swing (fact 10); the trade-offs are optical power budget and nanosecond photoconductor speed.

title: Printed-electronics nanoimprint access layer with 1% dead cells allowed
idea: Flexible-electronics makers accept defect rates an EUV fab never would. Pattern the access-transistor and buried-wordline layers by step-and-flash nanoimprint (~$1-2M tools vs ~$200M EUV) and treat the ~0.5-1% of defective or leaky access devices from template defects as a known error budget the page code absorbs.
why: Fact 4: removes 2-3 of the 5-7 EUV layers at the densest array levels, cutting capital and depreciation (~55% of wafer cost) perhaps 20-30%.

title: Substitute row-level refresh with mat-local segmented refresh for weak cells
idea: Substitute full-row (8 KB) refresh with sub-row refresh: hierarchical wordlines already have per-mat local drivers, so add a per-mat enable. Only the ~512-cell mats that hold profiled weak cells get the fast refresh rate; the rest of the row runs at a 4-8x longer interval.
why: Weak cells are sparse, so refreshing only their mats cuts tail refresh energy 16-64x versus row-granular retention-aware refresh, for a few gates per mat.

title: Sand-mold disposable cache: DRAM copies decay, nonvolatile pattern persists
idea: Like sand-casting molds broken after each pour while the pattern is kept, treat DRAM as a cache of clean lines backed by a dense nonvolatile master. Each line carries a restore timestamp. Lines past their certified retention are silently invalidated as misses instead of refreshed.
why: Zero refresh power. Capacity is spent only on lines being used, so DRAM needed per workload falls and the cost is an occasional refill from backing storage.

title: Substitute gas-exposed access modules with rare-gas-free certified process kit
idea: Substitute ad hoc process choices with a U.S. DPA/CHIPS-funded 'noble-gas-free access module': D2 anneal, thermal-ALD Mo gates, imprint/interference patterning and microwave activation, qualified as a drop-in kit any U.S. memory or foundry line can license, with shared reliability data on leakage tails.
why: Shields U.S. DRAM capacity from Qatar helium and neon supply shocks, lowers entry capital for new memory fabs, and shortens qualification by 1-2 years.

title: Circuit breakers, not fuses: resettable row repair held in MRAM
idea: Adapted from the move from one-time fuses to resettable breakers: replace laser-blown repair fuses with a small on-die MRAM remap table that can be rewritten without limit, so rows whose retention degrades or turns VRT are remapped, and later un-mapped, over the whole product life and through refurbishment.
why: Fuse and post-package repair are limited and mostly one-shot, so modules with drifting retention tails get scrapped; resettable repair keeps tail rows out of the refresh budget for life (fact 3) and makes refurbishment cheap.

title: Cell refreshes itself: storage-gated keeper on a pulsed restore rail
idea: Reverse who refreshes: instead of the periphery sensing and rewriting row by row, add a tiny second transistor to each cell whose gate is the storage node and whose channel links the node to a shared restore rail. Pulsing the rail to a boosted level (about VARY+Vt) tops up only cells still holding a '1' (their keeper is on) while '0' cells stay off, so one array-wide pulse refreshes millions of cells with no sense amps, no bitline swing and no bank lockout.
why: Refresh energy and time (fact 3): ~46 fJ/bit refresh shrinks to the few-fJ CV top-up of decayed charge, and the 10-20% refresh bandwidth loss goes to ~0; costs ~30-40% more cell area (2T1C).

title: Ga2O3 write transistor stacked over silicon read transistor
idea: Worse at 125 C: rely on IGZO, whose oxygen vacancies and hydrogen drift Vt when hot. Flip: a 2T gain cell with a laser-crystallized beta-Ga2O3 write device (4.8 eV gap, stable lattice) above a Si read FET, so the storage node sees a wide-gap off state while reads stay fast and non-destructive.
why: Refresh nearly removed at 125 C (fact 3) and avoids destructive read (fact 8).

title: Ultrawide-gap oxide gate storage removes capacitor, 32 deposited tiers
idea: IFR: the switch leaks so little that a transistor gate is the whole capacitor. An ALD ZnGa2O4/Ga2O3 write transistor (4.5-4.9 eV gap, off current ~1e-22 A) lets the ~0.1 fF gate of the read transistor hold charge for hours; with no capacitor each 2T0C layer is ~25 nm tall, so 32 tiers share one staircase and slit etch.
why: Constraint: removes the fact-1 capacitor and fact-3 refresh; 32 tiers at ~2x planar wafer cost and no EUV per tier give ~10x bits per dollar.

title: Resonant charge-recycling refresh through on-package LC tank
idea: Po: refresh pays for itself. During refresh bursts, bitline and wordline charge is swung adiabatically by a resonant inductor-capacitor tank (inductor built into the interposer) instead of being dumped to ground, so energy spent restoring one row is mostly recovered into the next row's precharge.
why: Fact 3 (~46 fJ/bit refresh) and fact 10 (CV^2 floor): adiabatic stepping cuts refresh energy 3-5x without touching the cell.

title: OS free-page list drives row-granular partial refresh
idea: Box: standard DRAM x standard access x standard sense x per-row refresh-enable bitmap inside the DRAM written by the OS allocator via mode-register commands x system x Si x zero masks. Freed or never-allocated pages stop being refreshed; the OS zeroes them on allocation anyway.
why: Servers often have 20-50% of DRAM free or reclaimable; row-level partial refresh cuts refresh power/bandwidth proportionally (fact 3).

title: Controller-only polarity steering: weak cells always store their discharged state
idea: 10-person constraint: with no process access, we exploit what we can learn about the cells. After profiling each row's true/anti-cell layout and weak cells, the controller picks one of a few per-row XOR masks (kept in a side table) so the row's weak cells always hold their discharged, non-leaking value. Rows whose weak cells are all parked empty drop to the slow refresh tier.
why: Fact 3: weak cells fail only when charged. Steering them to the empty state removes them from the refresh-setting tail and moves ~80%+ of weak rows to an interval of 1 s or more.

title: One-second dynamic NAND: leakage tuned to just-enough retention
idea: IFR: the barrier leaks exactly as much as the job allows. Build 3D-NAND-style vertical strings with a 2-2.5 nm tunnel oxide instead of ~6 nm so charge-trap cells write by direct tunneling at ~3-4 V in 10-50 ns, endure >1e14 cycles without Fowler-Nordheim damage and retain ~1 s; short 8-16-cell strings and SLC sensing aim reads near 100 ns.
why: Constraint: inherits 3D NAND's ~15x per-wafer bit density at NAND wafer cost, and 1 s retention means refresh 16x rarer than DRAM.

title: Spin-Hall-rotated half-metal spin valve as channel-free access gate
idea: Effect: spin Hall torque plus half-metallic spin filtering. Each cell's access element is a Co2MnSi/MgO/Co2MnSi junction; a current pulse in a BiSb topological-insulator wordline strip (no tungsten) exerts spin-orbit torque that rotates the row's free layers parallel (conducting) during access and antiparallel (no minority states at EF, blocking) during hold.
why: Leakage and wordline voltage (facts 3, 10): off-state set by spin polarization not temperature; row select by ~0.1 V current pulses instead of 3 V swings; 10-100x lower leakage if polarization >0.99.

title: Magnify barrier opacity: electron Bragg-mirror superlattice floating node
idea: Surround a charge-storage node with a Si/SiO2 (or ZnO/MgZnO) superlattice engineered so thermal electrons fall in a miniband gap and are reflected, while a ~2 V bias aligns a resonant miniband for ns-scale transport; zero-bias leakage is blocked without Fowler-Nordheim stress.
why: Flash-like retention with DRAM-like 10 ns writes and low oxide damage (endurance >>1e12 targeted); refresh-free.

title: LCD backplanes are already 1T1C DRAM: repurpose glass-panel fabs
idea: TRIZ #26 Copying: every LCD/OLED pixel is a thin-film transistor plus storage capacitor refreshed at 1-120 Hz, and LTPO oxide TFTs already hold charge at 1 Hz. Redesign Gen-6/8.5 glass backplanes at ~1 um rules into mm-scale memory tiles with LTPS periphery, stacked in several TFT tiers, refreshed at ~1 Hz instead of every 64 ms.
why: Capital intensity (Fact 4): display capex per m2 is orders of magnitude lower than DRAM capex per m2 and needs no EUV; refresh power becomes negligible (Fact 3). Density (~10-20 Mb/cm2 per tier) and TFT periphery speed limit it to CXL/capacity tiers.

title: Self-healing concrete capsules: buried hydrogen reservoir re-passivates interfaces
idea: Adapted from self-healing concrete, which embeds capsules that release healing agent into new cracks: deposit a deuterium-rich SiNx reservoir film above the access-device level, capped by a barrier with a controlled leak rate, so D slowly re-supplies the Si/SiO2 interface and re-passivates dangling bonds as they form over a 10-year life.
why: Interface-trap generation drives leakage-tail growth with age (fact 3); a built-in healing supply keeps retention stable for longer and makes modules fit for second-life reuse instead of scrap.

title: AMI VMOS revival: crystal-etched V-groove access transistors
idea: Revive 1970s VMOS, which American Microsystems used for memories: KOH anisotropic etching produces self-limiting {111} V-grooves whose geometry is set by the crystal, and epitaxial or diffusion depth sets the channel length. A uniform vertical access transistor forms with a U.S.-built 1X stepper and no EUV.
why: Crystal-defined geometry removes the CD variation that widens the Vt and leakage tail (fact 3), and avoids the single EUV supplier (fact 4).

title: Fridge-magnet doping: dopant-free charge-plasma access transistor
idea: Random stimulus 'fridge magnet': it holds by field, not glue. Make the array access transistor junctionless and implant-free: low-work-function metal contacts (e.g., Er/Hf silicide) electrostatically induce n-type source/drain in undoped silicon ('charge plasma'), and channel Vt comes from the gate metal work function rather than halo/well implants.
why: Each array implant needs litho, an SPM resist strip and a wet clean; deleting ~6 of them cuts array-FEOL UPW >10x, and with no metallurgical junction there is no junction leakage and the GIDL field is softer (fact 3).

title: Charge-plasma storage junction: no dopants, no implant damage
idea: Box: cap x access transistor whose storage-side n-region is induced electrostatically by a low-work-function metal contact and a positive fixed-charge dielectric instead of implanted phosphorus x SA x in-array x thin-body Si x ALD. With no metallurgical junction there is no end-of-range damage or dopant cluster to host trap-assisted tunneling.
why: Removes the main junction-leakage and GIDL tail sites (fact 3), aiming at ~10x tail reduction, and deletes implant steps.

title: Charge-plasma junctions: abundant-metal work functions replace implanted dopants
idea: Scale shift from implanted dopant atoms to an electric field: the access transistor's source/drain are induced electrostatically by low-work-function Mg- or Al-capped contacts (~3.7-4.1 eV) beside an undoped Si channel gated by a NiSi/TiN gate, so no metallurgical p-n junction sits at the storage node, which is the main seat of junction and trap-assisted leakage.
why: Junction leakage tail (fact 3): removes implant damage and dopant-related traps, ~5-10x lower junction leakage; no Hf, W or Co.

title: Dopant-free charge-plasma access transistor removes implant-driven leakage outliers
idea: Effect: work-function-induced charge plasma. Source/drain are induced electrostatically in an undoped channel by low-work-function (Hf-based) contacts, so there is no implanted metallurgical junction: no implant damage, no end-of-range defects and no random-dopant clusters that create the 13 fA outliers.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): narrows the retention distribution so refresh is set near the median, not the 1-ppm cell; claims 4-8x less refresh.

title: Deliberately weak canary cells trigger refresh per mat only when needed
idea: TRIZ #11 Beforehand cushioning: plant a sacrificial early warning. Each mat includes a few canary cells with ~50% of normal capacitance and a slightly leakier junction; a tiny always-on comparator polls them, and the mat is refreshed only when a canary flips, automatically tracking local temperature, voltage, aging and process corner (ECC backs up the rare cell weaker than its canary).
why: Most mats retain far longer than the 64 ms worst case (Fact 3): per-mat demand refresh claims 4-10x fewer refreshes at typical temperatures.

title: Cold-chain time-temperature indicator cells trigger refresh by accumulated thermal dose
idea: Vaccine shipments carry time-temperature indicators that integrate Arrhenius dose rather than trusting a schedule. In each subarray keep a few canary cells deliberately built leakier than the 6-sigma tail (wider junction implant); rewrite them at each refresh, poll them cheaply, and refresh the subarray only when a canary flips.
why: Spec refresh assumes 85 C worst case, but devices often run 45-65 C, so tracking real thermal dose cuts refresh 4-10x and most of the 16-33% idle refresh power (fact 3).

title: Silicon-nitride retention canary cells trigger refresh only when needed
idea: N: in every row, build one canary cell with the same DUV process but a deliberately trap-rich nitride liner at its storage contact so it leaks ~3x faster than the worst data cell; a small comparator flags when the canary drops below threshold and refreshes that row only, so refresh follows real temperature, aging and process.
why: Most rows retain >10x longer than the 64 ms spec (fact 3); hardware-ground-truth refresh could cut refresh operations 4-10x with no new litho capability.

title: Andon-cord canary cells trigger refresh only when truly needed
idea: Each subarray carries a few deliberately weak canary cells (thinner Cs or a leakier spacer), sensed continuously by a tiny comparator. Like a Toyota andon cord, a tripped canary pulls refresh for that subarray only, tracking real temperature and VRT state.
why: Fact 3: replaces the fixed 64/32 ms guardband with measured need, plausibly 2-4x fewer refreshes and matching recovered bandwidth.

title: Let the model refresh itself: compiler sweeps every weight row per window
idea: 10-person constraint: a compiler pass instead of hardware. For inference, place and stream the weights so every DRAM row holding weights is activated at least once per 32 ms; each read restores its row. The controller disables explicit refresh for those banks and falls back to REF only if a token stall exceeds the window.
why: Fact 3: weights are the majority of inference DRAM bytes, so their refresh energy and bandwidth drop to ~zero with only a compiler change and a controller flag.

title: Backlight-powered loadless latch on glass holds bits with photocurrent
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round: oxide TFTs are normally shielded from light because it raises leakage; instead deliberately bathe a transparent glass memory panel in steady dim backlight. Each cell is a cross-coupled n-type TFT pair whose high node is held up by a photodiode's photocurrent (replacing the pull-up of a loadless SRAM), tunable by light intensity to out-supply leakage at any temperature.
why: Refresh-free static storage with only n-type oxide TFTs, which lack a PMOS for normal SRAM (sidesteps Fact 3); backlight power is shared and dimmable.

title: Breathing cell plate: park stored charge at the leakage minimum
idea: Inverts 'the cell plate sits at a fixed VDD/2': in idle, ramp the common plate down ~0.3 V so '1' nodes sit lower (shrinking the GIDL and junction fields where the trap-assisted tail lives) while '0' nodes stay just short of forward bias, then ramp back before access; the stored difference is untouched because the plate shifts both states equally.
why: The tail's exponential field dependence (fact 3) gives ~3-10x longer idle retention, cutting self-refresh power proportionally with only a plate-driver change.

title: JEDEC refresh-hint command lets software own retention time
idea: Scale shift from silicon to standards: define a REFHINT/RETAIN command for DDR6, LPDDR6 and CXL.mem carrying per-range 'live until' and 'tolerates N errors' fields that DRAM self-refresh logic honours, plus a vendor-published per-bank retention-curve register.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3): makes software TTL and approximate regions portable across vendors, turning 2-5x refresh reductions into an ecosystem default.

title: Strontium titanate capacitor turns relaxed DUV pitch into 10x retention
idea: Sr: since a DUV-only cell is larger, spend the extra footprint on a planar or shallow-trench MIM capacitor of ALD SrTiO3 (k~100-200) instead of 60:1 pillars, storing 10-30 fF so the same fA leakage takes 3-6x longer to cross the sense margin.
why: Turns the no-EUV area penalty into charge (fact 1) and longer refresh intervals (fact 3) while avoiding extreme-aspect pillar etch; STO leakage and crystallization temperature are the risks.

title: Erasure decoding serves reads that collide with refresh
idea: Stagger refresh so only one chip in a rank refreshes at a time. A read that hits the refreshing chip is reconstructed from the other chips plus the ECC/parity chip, the way a RAID degraded read works.
why: Hides refresh stalls (10-20% bandwidth and tail latency at 32-64 Gb) using parity that ECC DIMMs already carry.

title: Complementary tunnel-FET static latch with attoamp hold current
idea: Po: SRAM that costs nothing to hold. Build a 4T cross-coupled latch from complementary vertical tunnel FETs whose band-to-band off-current is ~1e-17 A, monolithically stacked in two tiers over the access tier so a bit occupies ~8F^2; data is held statically and refresh disappears.
why: Facts 1 and 3: no capacitor and no refresh, with standby near mW per GB; risk is TFET on-current (read speed) and tier-stacking density.

title: TFET's weak drive is fine for DRAM access duty
idea: Tunnel FETs failed for logic because their band-to-band on-current was too low. A DRAM access device needs only ~1 uA to charge 5 fF in 5 ns. A line-tunneling TFET (gate-overlapped pocket) has no thermionic Boltzmann tail in the off state and only weak temperature dependence. A counter-doped drain pocket suppresses ambipolar leakage.
why: The leakage tail no longer doubles every ~10 C, so the 85 C double-refresh penalty disappears. Claimed 10x longer retention in hot servers, removing most of the 16-33% of idle power spent on refresh.

title: Vertical 3D charge-coupled shift-register memory with one regenerator per string
idea: Po: the bit is a rumor passed down a line. Store charge packets in potential wells along a tall vertical channel with dozens of stacked gate layers (3D NAND-like tiers clocked as a CCD); packets shift up and down and only the end-of-string regenerating sense amp restores them, so refresh is the shifting itself, with no per-bit capacitor or access transistor.
why: Facts 2, 4 and 7: reuses 3D NAND tier deposition (no EUV per tier, density scales with tier count); access becomes 100 ns-1 us block access, suited to tensor streams.

title: Substitute amorphous oxides with MBE-grown BaSnO3 perovskite channel
idea: Substitute amorphous oxide channels with La-doped BaSnO3 grown by MBE on a SrTiO3 buffer on Si (ultra-high vacuum, ozone oxidant, no carrier or sputter gas). It is a 3.1 eV-gap perovskite with film mobility above 100 cm^2/Vs, so on-current and off-leakage stop trading against each other.
why: At least 5x the on-current of IGZO at similar sub-aA leakage: shorter write times and refresh-light cells without large transistors.

title: Deuterium micro-heater self-anneal heals variable-retention trap cells in field
idea: H (as deuterium): package the die in a sealed D2-loaded cavity and embed polysilicon micro-heaters under each bank; when retention telemetry shows a bank's weak-cell count rising, its data is migrated out and the bank is held at ~300 C for seconds so deuterium re-passivates Si/SiO2 interface and GIDL traps (Si-D bonds resist hot-carrier breaking far better than Si-H).
why: Attacks the aging-driven growth of the trap-assisted leakage tail (fact 3); keeping tail cells healed over life could hold refresh at 2-4x longer intervals, cutting refresh energy ~50%.

title: Series-gated shared read channel: NAND-string gain cells
idea: IFR: many bits, one read transistor. Make 8-16 storage nodes the consecutive gate segments of a single vertical read channel; to read node k, plate lines capacitively boost every other node above threshold so the string current reports only node k's charge, while tiny vertical oxide write devices fill each node.
why: Constraint: per-bit read transistors and contacts disappear and 16 bits share one hole footprint, ~10x density at 3D NAND-like cost; non-destructive read also removes fact 8's restore writeback.

title: Substitute VDD/2 idle bitline with trimmed leakage-balance parking voltage
idea: Substitute the fixed VDD/2 standby bitline level with a parking voltage trimmed per subarray by an on-die DAC at test. It is set where channel leakage into the storage node offsets junction and GIDL leakage out of it for the weakest profiled cells.
why: Cuts the weakest cells' net leakage ~2-5x, extending the tail-limited refresh interval with existing devices and no new process step (so no rare gases).

title: Qubit dynamical decoupling applied to variable-retention-time traps
idea: Adapted from the dynamical-decoupling pulse trains that protect qubits from noise: VRT cells toggle between low and high leakage when one defect near the junction changes charge state, so short periodic pulses on the plate or well bias (every few microseconds, ~10 ns wide) reset that defect into its low-leakage state before it can switch.
why: VRT forces vendors to guard-band refresh 2-4x above static profiles because weak cells cannot be found reliably; pinning the traps would let profiled multi-rate refresh (fact 3) run safely, cutting refresh 2-4x.

title: Eliminate the Boltzmann limit: feedback-FET access device
idea: Use a gated p-i-n feedback FET whose intrinsic region holds charge barriers that collapse abruptly under positive feedback, giving <1 mV/dec switching. The device is hard off at 0 V gate and fully on near 1 V, so the 3 V wordline and the negative-wordline pump are removed.
why: Breaks the voltage floor (fact 10) and the leakage-vs-on-current tradeoff: ~1e-18 A off current at equal on current, wordline energy ~9x lower (3 V to 1 V), pump periphery area removed (fact 7).

title: Grid-leak self-biased wordlines replace the negative wordline pump
idea: Revive vacuum-tube grid-leak bias, in which a capacitor and leak resistor made a negative grid bias from the signal itself: each local wordline driver ends every activation by coupling its falling edge through a small MIM capacitor to undershoot below ground. The negative off-level relaxes slowly through a high-resistance leak, so recently used rows (hammer aggressors and their neighbors) sit deepest off.
why: Removes or shrinks the negative-wordline charge pump and its distribution in the periphery (fact 7), and deepens off-bias exactly where leakage and disturbance are worst (facts 3, 9).

title: Piano tuner's touch: per-cell threshold trim eliminates the wordline pump
idea: A piano tuner adjusts every string. At final test, a thin charge-trap layer in each access transistor's gate stack is programmed by Fowler-Nordheim pulses to center its threshold within +/-15 mV, collapsing the variation margin that forces VPP to ~3 V; the wordline then runs at VDD (1.1 V) directly, with no charge pump.
why: Pumps are ~30% efficient and energy goes as V^2: (3/1.1)^2 x ~3 is ~20x lower wordline energy per access, and the tight threshold spread also removes many tail cells.

title: Magnify demand signal: federal persistent-memory procurement on legacy U.S. fabs
idea: A CHIPS-style advance market commitment obliges federal datacenters to buy a quota of U.S.-made non-volatile working memory (SiC, AFE, LiNbO3 or MRAM flavors) built on 28-90 nm domestic legacy lines that need no EUV.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital intensity: legacy-line conversions ~$1-2B vs $15B+ for a new DRAM fab; seeds domestic supply.

title: Downhole adaptive code rate: parity grows as the die heats
idea: Oil-well tools swing 25-200 C and cannot afford refresh that doubles every ~10 C. Keep refresh fixed and let raw BER float from 0.01% up to 1%; an on-die thermometer steps each page's code rate from 0.97 down to 0.85, borrowing spare capacity from a reserved pool when hot.
why: Fact 3: refresh energy stays flat across temperature instead of rising 4-8x when hot; capacity rather than energy absorbs heat, which suits AI servers running memory at 85-95 C.

title: Substitute linear gate dielectric with antiferroelectric ZrO2 steep-switch stack
idea: Substitute the HfO2/SiO2 gate stack with antiferroelectric ZrO2. Its field-induced AFE-to-FE transition gives a transient negative-capacitance boost at turn-on, then relaxes fully to zero polarization at zero field: no remanence and none of the wake-up or fatigue of ferroelectric gates.
why: Sub-60 mV/dec turn-on allows a higher Vt and lower VPP: target ~10x lower leakage or ~1 V less wordline, without ferroelectric endurance limits.

title: Antiferroelectric latent-charge buffer holds stored-1 voltage on a plateau
idea: Reverse the capacitor dielectric's role from passive to defending its charge: use ZrO2-rich antiferroelectric HZO and bias the plate so a stored '1' sits just above the AFE back-switching voltage. As leakage drains the node, AFE domains switch back and release bound polarization charge (~10-20 uC/cm2), pinning the voltage on a plateau the way latent heat holds ice water at 0 C.
why: Retention and charge wall (facts 1, 3): effective capacitance at the hold point rises 5-10x, so retention rises ~5x without taller pillars; AFE has no remanent polarization, avoiding the fatigue/imprint of prior HZO FeRAM concepts.

title: Antiferroelectric back-switching plateau acts as a constant-voltage charge reservoir
idea: Add a thin antiferroelectric ZrO2 film in parallel with the storage dielectric. Size it so the written '1' voltage is above its field-induced polar switching and its back-switching edge sits just above the sense threshold. As leakage drains the node, the AFE back-switches and releases ~10-20 uC/cm^2 of polarization charge at a nearly constant voltage, pinning the node like a clamped reservoir.
why: Usable charge above the sense threshold rises several-fold without taller pillars. That attacks fact 1 and the retention equation t = dQ/I (fact 3), for 3-5x retention at equal leakage.

title: Probe-style closed-loop power control applied to refresh pacing
idea: Space probes tune transmit power from receiver feedback to sit just above the error target. Make each row group's refresh period a control loop: the decoder reports corrected-bit counts per page, and the controller lengthens or shortens that group's period to hold raw BER near a 0.5-1% setpoint, following temperature, aging and VRT without profiling.
why: Fact 3: refresh follows each group's real decay instead of the global worst case, about 2x below a fixed 1%-quantile schedule, with built-in safety.

title: Antiferroelectric capacitor pins stored-one voltage as charge reservoir
idea: Effect: antiferroelectric double-hysteresis switching. The cell capacitor uses AFE ZrO2 with plate bias set so a stored '1' sits just above the backward switching field; as leakage drains charge, polarization release (~2Pr x area, ~10x the linear charge) holds the node near that voltage, which stays above the sense threshold, and reads look like normal charge sharing. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Capacitor charge wall and leakage (facts 1, 3): effective storage charge ~10x, retention ~5-10x. Risk: AFE endurance toward 1e15 cycles.

title: Pinned-photodiode storage well from 180 nm image-sensor fabs
idea: Fuse the CIS 4T pixel with a DRAM cell. Charge sits in a fully depleted buried n-well whose surface is pinned by p+, away from the Si/SiO2 interface, and is read by a transfer gate onto a floating diffusion and source follower. This is built on existing 180 nm CIS lines.
why: Pinned-well dark current is ~10 e-/s against ~1e5 e-/s for DRAM junctions, so retention runs seconds to minutes with no refresh. The read is gain-based and non-destructive.

title: Elastic twin-cell rows: trade capacity for retention on demand
idea: Reverse one-cell-per-bit into two-cells-per-bit at run time: a decoder change in DRAM built on existing mature lines lets the controller pair a row with its twin across the open-bitline sense amps and store complementary charge, so the amplifier sees a full differential instead of a half signal. Regions switched to twin mode (phone standby, long-lived cold data) lose half their capacity but retain ~4-10x longer.
why: Self-refresh power in idle regions (fact 3) drops 4-10x; design-only change in existing DRAM fabs.

title: Refresh fixed at one second: sense amps flag low-confidence bits
idea: Limit: the refresh interval is forced to 1 s and the cell cannot improve. Add a dual-reference margin check to the sense amp (a second sense against a shifted reference) so cells whose signal sits near the decision point are flagged as erasures. The ECC decoder can then correct about twice as many errors, because an erasure costs half a correction.
why: Fact 3: knowing where the weak bits are doubles effective correction power, making 1 s refresh tolerable and cutting refresh energy and bandwidth ~15x.

title: Thousand tiny tapeouts: crowdsourced access-device leakage variants on open PDKs
idea: 10-person constraint: crowdsource the search a small team cannot fund. Publish an open eDRAM access-device test-cell template for open-PDK shuttles (SKY130, GF180, IHP SG13G2). Pay bounties to hobbyists and students whose variants (gate shapes, well-bias tricks, guard rings, stacked devices) beat the baseline in silicon-measured retention, ranked by an automated FPGA tester.
why: Fact 3: hundreds of cheap parallel experiments explore leakage geometry faster than one team could, and the winners feed tail-reduction techniques into licensable IP.

title: Polarization-doped AlGaN access channel eliminates random dopant fluctuation
idea: Al: build the access transistor in a compositionally graded AlGaN layer whose polarization gradient creates fixed 3D charge (polarization doping) instead of impurity atoms, so channel and junction 'doping' is set by a continuous Al-fraction grade identical in every cell.
why: Random dopant fluctuation in ~20 nm channels is a principal source of the Vt spread that makes the 13 fA tail (fact 3); dopant-free channels could tighten sigma-Vt ~2x and extend refresh 2-4x, if GaN-on-Si dislocation leakage is tamed.

title: Polarity-aware scrambling keeps most cells in the uncharged state
idea: Only charged cells decay, and 'charged' means '1' in true cells and '0' in anti-cells. Learn each row's true/anti layout with a one-time retention test. Then XOR each 64 B line with that map, plus a per-line inversion bit chosen to minimize charged cells, so zero-heavy data leaves most capacitors empty. Firmware and FPGA work, <$300k.
why: The charged-cell fraction drops from ~50% to ~10-40% depending on data. Decay-error rate falls in proportion, so ECC-backed refresh intervals can stretch further (fact 3).

title: Rubber vulcanization: sulfur-healed MoS2 vertical access channels at back-end temperature
idea: Vulcanization uses sulfur to cure rubber's weak links. Grow bilayer MoS2 by MOCVD from Mo(CO)6 and H2S at <=450 C on the capacitor top as a vertical access channel, 'vulcanize' its sulfur vacancies (the dominant trap and leakage path) with an in-situ H2S anneal, and encapsulate with ALD alumina from TMA/water instead of fluoropolymer passivation.
why: A ~1.6 eV gap and sub-1 nm junctionless body give orders lower off-current than silicon (fact 3) and allow monolithic stacking of access layers (fact 2), fluorine-free end to end.

title: Ripstop Z-channel codes let decayed ones be woven back
idea: Like ripstop nylon's reinforcing threads stopping tears, encode rows with asymmetric Z-channel / constant-weight codes built for one-way 1->0 decay. Leaked ones become known-direction erasures that are corrected and rewritten on read.
why: Zero refresh for data read within the extended window: the usable unrefreshed lifetime grows from ~64 ms to several seconds, covering most transient AI data with no refresh energy.

title: Reverse the e-waste flow: profile and redeploy retired server DRAM
idea: Flip decommissioned DIMMs from shredder back to rack: test pulled DDR4/DDR5 modules on existing ATE for per-row retention and error history, sort them into retention grades, and redeploy them in CXL memory-expander pools whose controller applies per-row multi-rate refresh and assigns weak rows to spare or short-lived buffer duty.
why: Raises usable memory supply with zero fab capacity (hyperscalers retire many PB per year) while retention-graded refresh keeps energy per bit acceptable (fact 3).

title: Intrinsic carriers below one per chip: amorphous Ga2O3 access channel
idea: Limit: the channel's intrinsic carrier density must make thermal leakage physically negligible. Use ALD amorphous Ga2O3 (Eg ~4.8 eV, no indium) as a BEOL access-transistor channel, with source/drain doped by oxygen vacancies from a local H2 plasma. The theoretical off-current floor is ~1e-24 A/um, orders of magnitude below IGZO.
why: Fact 3 and resources: refresh-free retention of hours or more at 85 C, no exposure to indium supply concentration, and the device stacks in BEOL for 3D tiers (fact 2). Risk: mobility below 5 cm2/Vs demands a short channel.

title: Nextreme thin-film thermoelectrics revived to dodge 85C refresh doubling
idea: Nextreme's thin-film thermoelectric coolers faded because of poor efficiency. Refresh doubles above 85 C, so even a low-COP cooler pays off if it shaves the last 5-10 C. Screen-print Bi2Te3-based thermoelectric films onto DIMM and HBM heat spreaders and turn them on only when the die sensors approach 80 C.
why: Keeps hot accelerator memory in 1x refresh, avoiding the extra ~46 fJ/bit of refresh and ~10% of bandwidth that 2x refresh costs. Printable and cheap.

title: Thermos vacuum-gap field-emission access switch
idea: Random stimulus 'thermos flask': its vacuum blocks heat, so a sealed 4-6 nm vacuum gap blocks charge. The access device is a wordline-gated nano-emitter (low-work-function LaB6 or Cs-dosed tip) facing the storage node; off-state current is Fowler-Nordheim-limited to essentially zero, and raising the gate field opens a ~uA emission pulse for read/write.
why: Removes subthreshold, GIDL and junction leakage paths at once (fact 3): retention limited only by capacitor dielectric, refresh interval 100x+ longer, ~46 fJ/bit refresh energy nearly eliminated.

title: Graded work-function wordline flattens the GIDL hotspot
idea: Scale shift into a nanometre composition profile: deposit the buried wordline as a laterally graded TiN-to-TiAlN stack (composition changing over ~10-20 nm) so the gate work function is lower facing the storage node and higher at the channel centre, reducing the gate-to-drain field that drives band-to-band tunnelling while keeping Vt high.
why: GIDL tail (fact 3): ~20-30% lower peak field gives ~10x lower GIDL and permits a smaller negative wordline bias (fact 10).

title: Ferroelectric-semiconductor alpha-In2Se3 channel as its own memory
idea: Po: the channel remembers which way it points. Make the transistor channel from the ferroelectric semiconductor alpha-In2Se3, whose out-of-plane polarization flips with a gate pulse and modulates channel conductance; there is no separate ferroelectric layer or capacitor, and read is nondestructive.
why: Facts 1, 3 and 8: capacitorless, refresh-free, nondestructive low-voltage bit beyond the HZO prior; risk is endurance and CMOS-compatible In2Se3 deposition.

title: Orphaned flexible-display pilot lines become a national printed memory foundry
idea: U.S. flexible display programs, such as the Army-funded Flexible Display Center, never found an anchor product. Re-task such roll-to-roll oxide-TFT lines into a federally backed pilot foundry for refresh-free oxide memory foils, with DoD as anchor buyer for low-power ruggedized memory.
why: Supplies the anchor customer whose absence killed U.S. flexible electronics, and creates U.S.-made DRAM-adjacent capacity without $15B fabs or EUV.

title: Williams tube reborn: MEMS electron beams paint charge on film
idea: Inverts 'every bit needs a transistor': like the 1947 Williams-Kilburn tube, store bits as charge spots on a continuous unpatterned dielectric film, written and read by secondary emission from an array of ~10^4 microfabricated field-emitter beamlets each scanning a ~100 um patch; the beam re-scan doubles as refresh.
why: Cost per bit falls to film coating plus the amortized emitter array, ~100x cheaper per GB claimed; trade-off: us latency, vacuum packaging, emitter lifetime.

title: Antioxidant hydrogen-scavenger layer guards oxide-channel access transistors
idea: Cells use catalase and glutathione to sacrificially mop up reactive species before they damage DNA; pattern a hydrogen-gettering film (Ti-rich TiNx or an oxygen-rich ZrOx sink) next to but isolated from the In2O3/InGaZnO channel so it irreversibly traps hydrogen diffusing from later PECVD SiN and BEOL dielectrics at <=400 C.
why: Hydrogen donors cause negative Vt shift and the high-leakage tail in oxide FETs; scavenging keeps off-current near 1e-19 A/um array-wide, so BEOL cells retain for >10 s and refresh energy falls ~100x.

title: Deep boron barrier implant blocks substrate diffusion leakage
idea: Box: standard cap x standard access x SA x in-array x Si x one high-energy implant mask placing a p+ layer ~0.5-1 um below the array. Its built-in field reflects electrons diffusing from the substrate and periphery (including sense-amp hot-carrier emission) away from storage nodes.
why: Diffusion current dominates at 85-95C; blocking it gives ~2x hot retention (fact 3) and less periphery-induced disturb for one mask.

title: Area-selective deposition self-aligns every tier's access gate
idea: IFR: each tier's transistor assembles itself where it belongs. Inhibitor SAMs that bind everywhere except exposed oxide-semiconductor edges inside the slit let area-selective ALD grow gate dielectric and gate metal only on channel edges, in all tiers at once, with no per-tier lithography or overlay.
why: Constraint: removes the per-tier patterning that makes 3D DRAM costly (facts 2 and 4), so ~30 tiers cost mostly deposition time, about 2.5x planar cost for ~10x bits per dollar.

title: SESO memory reborn on 2 nm single-crystal silicon nanosheets
idea: Hitachi's SESO used ~3 nm polysilicon channels: quantum confinement widened the bandgap and cut leakage to ~1e-19 A, but grain boundaries made devices variable and slow. Thin single-crystal SOI nanosheets to 2 nm with self-limiting low-temperature plasma oxidation, which raises the effective gap to ~1.6-1.8 eV. Raised epitaxial source/drain recovers the on-current.
why: Access-transistor off-current of ~1e-19 A, 5-6 decades below the 13 fA tail, made with silicon tooling. Refresh becomes ~1000x rarer and its share of idle power drops to near zero.

title: Weak-cell exile: banish leakage-tail cells to a tiny SRAM
idea: Profile per-cell retention at test and periodically in the field, remap the ~0.01-0.1% of cells with retention <1 s into an on-die SRAM/CAM patch table keyed by address, and refresh the remaining 99.9% at 1 s instead of 64 ms. Online re-profiling catches variable-retention-time cells.
why: Minifying who sets the refresh rate magnifies the interval ~16x: refresh energy and bandwidth tax down ~16x for <0.5% die area.

title: Thin-film Peltier layer in HBM base die cools the array
idea: Effect: Peltier thermoelectric cooling. Bi2Te3/Sb2Te3 superlattice pads between the base logic die and the lowest DRAM die, plus over hotspot columns, pump heat to the lid only when the stack exceeds ~80 C, holding array temperature ~10 C lower (retention roughly doubles per 10 C). DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Refresh bandwidth (fact 3): avoids the 2x refresh regime above 85 C (10-20% bandwidth); costs some pump power.

title: Water-utility night pressure reduction: idle-mode rebias of array wells
idea: Adapted from utilities that lower mains pressure at night because leakage scales with pressure: when the DRAM enters self-refresh, it raises the array p-well bias toward 0 V (cutting the storage-junction field that drives trap-assisted leakage) and deepens the wordline-off voltage to hold subthreshold leakage, then restores active-mode biases on exit.
why: Active-mode biases are chosen for speed and row-hammer margin; idle mode can sit at the leakage minimum. Junction-field relief can cut tail leakage 2-5x, stretching self-refresh intervals proportionally (fact 3) at no area cost.

title: Minify idle power to zero: park non-volatile memory ranks fully off
idea: Because NV working memory keeps data unpowered, the hypervisor consolidates hot pages and cuts power entirely (not just refresh) to idle ranks within microseconds, so a power-capped rack can install ~2x more memory at the same watts.
why: Removes refresh and standby power completely and converts power-limited deployments into more usable memory.

title: XeF2-carved vacuum gap isolates storage node from passing wordline
idea: Xe: deposit a sacrificial Si or Ge spacer between the storage-node contact and the adjacent passing buried wordline, then release it with XeF2 vapor (near-infinite selectivity to oxide/nitride) through a small vent, leaving a sealed k=1 vacuum gap that weakens passing-gate field and coupling at the storage junction.
why: Passing-wordline fields drive GIDL and row-hammer charge pumping (facts 3, 9); a k=1 gap versus nitride (k~7) cuts coupling ~5x, plausibly 3-10x lower passing-gate leakage and a higher hammer threshold.

title: Engineered single border trap per cell as atomic-scale bit
idea: Po: the defect that causes leakage is the memory. Place one deep border trap per minimum-size transistor by single-ion implantation and use its occupancy, which shifts Vt by tens of mV in a ~10 nm device just as random telegraph noise does, as the stored bit; write by gate-bias pulse, read by drain current.
why: Facts 1 and 3: the smallest conceivable capacitorless cell, with retention set by trap emission time (designable ms to s); speculative because single-trap placement and read margin are hard.

title: Store less charge to keep more: low-field hold during self-refresh
idea: Reverse the instinct to store maximum charge: in self-refresh, restore '1's to ~0.7 V instead of ~1.0 V and set plate and negative wordline so the gate-to-storage-node field is minimal. GIDL and trap-assisted tunneling fall exponentially with field while charge falls only ~30%, so GIDL-limited tail cells hold longer; one full-swing pass restores normal margin on wake.
why: Self-refresh power (fact 3, 16-33% of idle): if tail leakage drops >3x for 30% less charge, the interval can double while each refresh costs ~50% less CV2 energy (fact 10).

title: Compressed packing fills freed rows with leak-aligned padding
idea: The controller compresses pages, packs them into fewer rows, and writes the freed rows entirely with each cell type's leak-direction value (0 for true cells, 1 for anti-cells). A per-row flag marks those rows refresh-exempt until reallocated.
why: With ~2x compressibility, 40-50% of rows need no refresh, cutting refresh energy ~40%, and the same packing also yields capacity.

title: Minify the refreshed footprint: compress-then-park unrefreshed rows
idea: The memory controller compresses cold pages (base-delta/LZ, ~2-3x) into packed regions and disables refresh on the vacated rows using subarray-granular partial-array self-refresh, so the refreshed footprint shrinks with the data.
why: Refresh energy scales with refreshed rows: 2-3x lower idle refresh power, plus freed capacity.

title: Compress rows and pad with discharged cells that cannot decay
idea: Po: most memory is empty. The controller compresses each row, writes the payload into the fewest cells, fills the rest with the discharged state (which in true cells cannot leak into an error) and picks per-row polarity so most bits sit in the safe state; rows flagged all-safe skip refresh.
why: Fact 3: only charged cells need refresh; with ~2x compressibility and polarity choice, 50-70% of charged cells vanish and many rows skip refresh entirely.

title: Hot-mode compression consolidates data before partial-array self-refresh
idea: Worse at 125 C: refresh every bank at the 4-8x hot rate even when half the data is compressible. Flip: when the die crosses 105 C, the controller compresses cold pages 2-3x into a subset of banks and power-gates the rest, so hot refresh covers fewer rows.
why: Hot self-refresh energy (fact 3) down 50-65%.

title: Battery direct recycling for dies: harvest and re-bond onto new base dies
idea: Adapted from direct cathode recycling, which restores battery material instead of smelting it: debond DRAM dies from retired modules, thin and retest them, then hybrid-bond them onto a new logic base die that holds a per-row retention map and issues row-specific refresh, so dies with drifted leakage run again behind a smarter refresh engine.
why: Reuses the most capital-heavy part, the EUV-patterned array (fact 4), and compensates aged access devices (fact 3) with new logic; each reused die avoids new fab capacity.

title: Flip the stack so memory dies, not logic, touch the cold plate
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: use the vertical heat path instead of fighting it in-plane. In HBM and 3D stacks, place the DRAM dies against the cold plate and route the logic base-die heat out through a separate high-conductivity path (thermal TSV bundles plus a backside spreader), so the memory runs ~20-30 C cooler; cell leakage roughly halves every ~10 C.
why: Refresh rate doubles above 85 C today (Fact 3): 4-8x lower cell leakage lets HBM leave 2x refresh mode, regaining up to 10-20% bandwidth.

title: Penguin-huddle thermal rotation of long-lived data in HBM stacks
idea: Emperor penguins rotate so no bird stays on the cold edge too long; the HBM controller maps long-lived data (weights, KV cache) to the coolest dies far from the logic base and short-lived activations to the hottest dies, and runs a separate temperature-graded refresh rate per die.
why: Stacks have 10-20 C gradients; refreshing cool dies at half rate and hot dies only for data that outlives retention cuts stack refresh energy ~30-50% without new devices.

title: Aerogel thermal break keeps HBM DRAM cores 15C cooler
idea: Box: standard HBM core dies x standard access x standard sense x silica-aerogel or porous-polymer layer between hot logic base die and core stack, with logic heat routed through dedicated copper thermal TSVs to the lid x package x Si x zero masks. Core dies then sit near cold-plate temperature instead of the logic hotspot.
why: Retention halves per ~10C; a 15C drop gives ~3x longer refresh interval, reclaiming HBM bandwidth and power (facts 3, 6).

title: Boron arsenide spreader flattens hotspots so refresh tracks average temperature
idea: B: bond a cubic boron arsenide layer (thermal conductivity ~1,300 W/m-K) between the DRAM die and the hot logic or HBM base die, shrinking intra-die temperature gradients from ~10-15 C to ~2 C, so the refresh rate, which is set by the hottest mat, can be specified for the mean temperature.
why: Refresh interval is dictated by worst-temperature cells (fact 3); removing a 10 C hotspot roughly halves the required refresh rate in HBM stacks above accelerators, recovering bandwidth and ~10% idle power.

title: Furnace refractory lining: thermal break shields HBM from hot logic
idea: Like a refractory firebrick lining, insert a low-k porous thermal-break layer between the logic base die and the DRAM stack. Logic heat is routed around the DRAM through peripheral copper thermal columns to the lid.
why: Leakage roughly doubles every ~10 C. Keeping HBM 20 C cooler cuts refresh rate ~4x and lifts bandwidth.
